title: Spinoza's calm
hook: Spinoza, not a Stoic, also taught that understanding our emotions' causes makes us freer (Ethics 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Justus Lipsius and Neostoicism, writing through Europe's religious wars, and the old Stoic word constancy. Did one storm come your way, and did you stay steady inside it? Day six hundred sixty-two.

Holland, the 1660s. A man sits at a bench grinding glass lenses for microscopes and telescopes, slow work, the kind where a rushed hand ruins the piece. Alongside the lenses, he is writing a book laid out like a geometry textbook: definitions, axioms, propositions, proofs. It's about God, nature and the human mind, and its last part is about something very ordinary: how to be a little less pushed around by your own feelings. His name is Baruch Spinoza. He wasn't a Stoic, and he said so. But today he sits on the porch's front step for a while.
screen: `HOLLAND, A LENS GRINDER'S BENCH.` → `A BOOK BUILT LIKE GEOMETRY.` → `NOT A STOIC, BUT CLOSE BY.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Spinoza's Ethics was published in 1677, the year he died. Its fourth part is titled, in the old English translations, Of Human Bondage: what it's like to be dragged along by passions you don't understand. The fifth part is about freedom. Second, the idea. Early in part five, Spinoza argues that a feeling which is a passion, something that just happens to us, stops being a passion once we form a clear and distinct idea of it. Put plainly: when you understand where a feeling comes from, its causes, it has less hold on you. Not because you crushed it, but because you saw it. Anger at your sister turns out to be tiredness, an old childhood hurt, and a missed lunch, all at once. Seen whole, it shrinks to its real size. Third, where he parts from the Stoics. In the preface to that same part, Spinoza names them directly. The Stoics, he says, thought our feelings depend entirely on our will, so that we could command them completely. Even they, he notes, had to admit from experience that it takes long practice. Spinoza goes further: the will alone isn't the tool. Understanding is. So this is a neighbor, not a member: close to Epictetus's idea that it's our judgments that disturb us, but built on different ground. Fourth, why it helps on a Tuesday. You can't always change a feeling by deciding to. But you can almost always get curious about it. Where did this come from? What's underneath? Curiosity is a kind of distance, and a little distance is a kind of freedom.
screen: `ETHICS, 1677: BONDAGE, THEN FREEDOM.` · `SEE A FEELING'S CAUSE, IT LOOSENS.` · `NOT WILLPOWER: UNDERSTANDING.` · `CURIOSITY IS A KIND OF DISTANCE.` · then, large: `UNDERSTAND IT.`

segments.voice: Pick one feeling that's been with you today. Irritation, worry, a low hum of sadness, anything. Don't try to get rid of it. Just name it. Now, slowly, ask where it came from. Not one cause; let a few show up. Something someone said. How you slept. Something older than today. Lay them out in your mind like lenses on a bench. Notice whether the feeling changes size as you look. If it doesn't, that's fine too. You're only looking. The bell holds the time.
Spinoza's calm: not a feeling switched off, but a feeling understood, its causes seen clearly, so it pushes you around a little less. Today's word.
Your line: understand it. The next time a strong feeling arrives today, before you act on it, ask one curious question: what caused this? Day six hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Spinoza often treat a strong emotion as something to understand rather than fight, tracing its causes until it loosens its grip.

fork.setup: you're furious and can't talk yourself out of it. what would Spinoza try?
options: trace where the anger came from
fork.reveal: for Spinoza, a feeling understood through its causes loses its hold on us; understanding, not willpower, is the tool.

original.note: Latin, Spinoza's word in the Ethics for an emotion or feeling.

trapdoor: what you thought: stay calm by keeping your feelings under control.
what it means: understand a feeling's causes clearly and it has less power over you.
what a scholar hears: Ethics 5, proposition 3: an affect that is a passion ceases to be one once we form a clear and distinct idea of it; the preface to part 5 criticizes the Stoics by name.

notes: Ethics 5 prop. 3 paraphrased (an emotion which is a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it). Confirm.

Ethics 5 preface: Spinoza says the Stoics thought emotions depend absolutely on our will and we can command them absolutely, but that experience forced them to admit much practice is needed. Confirm the paraphrase.
Part 4 title 'Of Human Bondage' follows the Elwes (1883) English rendering; Latin 'De Servitute Humana'.
Spinoza ground lenses for a living (commonly reported); in the 1660s he lived in Rijnsburg and Voorburg, later The Hague; hook says Holland.
Ethics published posthumously in 1677 (Opera Posthuma). Confirm.
Reviewer edit: the teach now says the Stoics themselves admitted long practice was needed (as in the preface), rather than presenting that as Spinoza's counter-argument.
How much Spinoza owed to Stoicism is debated by scholars; the script says only that he named and criticized them. Confirm 'he said so' is fair.
10% audit (year 2): hook's invented detail 'in the evenings he writes' changed to 'alongside the lenses, he is writing'; nothing records when in the day he wrote.
